source_edits.old: Cryptographic artifacts such as hashes, nonces and ciphertexts are readily recognizable in their usual textual forms. RankCloak conceals this syntax by mapping serialized artifacts to language-model token ranks and expressing them as generated cover text. Its bounded codecs and segmented generation provide a reproducible framework for studying recovery, efficiency and contextual acceptability. Across 480 deterministic artifacts from eight classes, three model families and 18 English prompts, all 6,480 primary trials recovered the original bytes under preserved token sequences and shared configurations. In a contextual evaluation with blinded model judges, 537 of 576 message pairs had complete ratings. Automated acceptance reached 90.3\% for RankCloak and 96.6\% for matched greedy ordinary output under a rubric allowing minor awkwardness. Entropy gating reduced selected detection signals, with tradeoffs in payload rate and completion. Visible-text retokenization recovered 88 of 144 covers, while transformations and configuration mismatches exposed transport sensitivity. Steganalysis remained effective, and surface concealment does not imply undetectability or confidentiality. These results establish artifact specific concealment and configured recovery, with quantified efficiency, acceptability and transport tradeoffs that inform the design of language-model-based information hiding.
source_edits.new: Cryptographic artifacts such as hashes, nonces, identifiers, and ciphertexts are conspicuous when transmitted in their usual textual forms. RankCloak conceals this recognizable form by encoding each synthetic artifact through language model token choices, producing cover text that does not directly display the artifact. We evaluated 480 public deterministic artifacts from eight classes with three open source model families and 18 English prompt templates. The decoder recovered every artifact across 6,480 primary trials when the original token sequence and shared generation configuration were preserved. Recovery from rendered cover text succeeded in 61.1 percent of the tested robustness sample, whereas the tested blockquote and trimming operation, paraphrasing, and decoding with another model failed. Stronger detection tests separated duplicate and near-duplicate material before training, withheld model families, included human written comparisons, and used probabilities from the generating model. Under these tests, encoded covers were often detectable. Restricting embedding to positions with several plausible next words reduced some detection signals but also reduced capacity and increased cover length. Detecting a possible encoding does not itself display or reconstruct the concealed artifact. RankCloak demonstrates concealment and recovery specifically for cryptographic artifacts under a shared configuration while exposing detectability and transmission limitations, but it does not establish the concealment of arbitrary natural-language messages.

source_edits.old: The intact-message study extends evaluation from diagnostics at token level to automated contextual acceptability. Under a rubric accepting understandable text with minor awkwardness, the panel accepted 90.3\% of encoded messages and 96.6\% of matched greedy controls. The -6.3 percentage-point difference quantifies a remaining acceptability cost alongside the high acceptance level of encoded messages. These are model judgments of complete delivered conditions, with possible contributions from length and content differences. They do not establish human acceptance or indistinguishability. The historical likelihood analysis provides complementary evidence about local fixed-path compatibility.
source_edits.new: The intact-message study extends token-level diagnostics with an automated evaluation of contextual coherence and acceptability. Under a common rubric accepting understandable text with minor awkwardness, the blinded panel accepted 90.3\% of encoded messages and 96.6\% of matched greedy controls. Most encoded messages were therefore judged understandable in their supplied contexts, while the paired difference of -6.3 percentage points quantifies the remaining difference from ordinary output. The comparison evaluates complete delivered messages, including their length and content differences. The historical likelihood analysis provides complementary evidence about local fixed-path compatibility.

answer_edits.old: The new study applies the same lenient, fixed rubric to complete encoded messages and matched greedy ordinary controls. It uses authentic prompts, blinded judges from other model families, a separate constructed calibration set and a frozen 48-payload sample. Among 537 complete message pairs in 280 trials, the equally weighted panel accepts 90.3 [88.4, 92.1]% of encoded messages and 96.6 [95.0, 98.1]% of matched ordinary messages. The paired difference is -6.3 [-8.7, -3.9] percentage points. Brackets give 95% payload-cluster intervals stratified by class. Mean logical connectedness is 3.60/5 for encoded text and 4.00/5 for ordinary text. Binary judge disagreement is 14.6% and 6.7%, respectively. The previous fragment assays are retained as supplementary methodological history, with their failed semantic control checks and limited local likelihood findings. Historical recovery, transport, entropy, quantization and detector results are unchanged. No reader validation, confidentiality or indistinguishability is claimed.

answer_edits.old:
A seeded selection covers 48 payloads across four hexadecimal classes, three generators and two schedules, giving 576 messages outside the earlier scored cohort. Each is paired with ordinary output from the same generator and prompt using matched filtering, greedy continuation, budget and stopping rules. Among 537 complete pairs, panel acceptance is 90.3% for RankCloak and 96.6% for ordinary output. The paired difference is -6.3 percentage points with a 95% payload-cluster interval of [-8.7, -3.9]. Mean logical connectedness is 3.60/5 versus 4.00/5.

Messages are averaged within trials and payloads, with intervals conditional on the fixed reused controls. Supplementary Note S20 reports calibration mistakes, the 39 incomplete pairs, missing-score sensitivity, subgroup results, disagreement and exact unfavorable examples. Judges and generators are not fully crossed, and the comparison does not isolate a causal boundary effect. This provides automated evidence of contextual acceptability, not measured human perception or indistinguishability. The earlier fragment pilots and limited likelihood evidence remain in S17. The editor can assess whether this evidence meets the requested validation.
